_meta.how_to_read: sequence lists one main crop per year, repeating after the last year. 'fallow' means the field is left unsown for that season. second_crops are optional summer crops sown right after a winter crop in the same year (only where the season is long enough and water is available). regions use the 7 geographic regions of Turkey; irrigation is rainfed, irrigated or either.
_meta.source: Common rotation patterns in Turkish agriculture compiled by the team from general agronomy references; not yet validated by a local expert.

rotations.notes: Traditional dryland system: the fallow year stores rain in the soil, but leaves it bare and open to erosion.
Cold high plateaus (Erzurum, Kars, Ağrı, Ardahan): wheat is sown in spring because winters are too harsh; fallow stores water.
A legume in the middle year breaks the cereal run and adds nitrogen.
Vetch replaces fallow: soil stays covered in winter and the legume adds nitrogen, at the cost of some stored water.
Drought-tolerant oilseed as a non-cereal break crop.
Classic Southeastern Anatolia system with winter-sown red lentil.
Dominant rotation in Thrace.
Adds a winter brassica break crop to the Thrace system.
Çukurova and Harran pattern: wheat, then second-crop maize in summer, then cotton.
Breaks continuous cotton with a cereal and a legume.
Four-year gap between beet crops limits beet nematode; legume year rebuilds nitrogen.
Niğde-Nevşehir style: potato, a cereal break, then a legume.
Field tomato followed by a cereal; avoids nightshade back to back.
Three alfalfa years build soil and nitrogen for the cereals that follow.
Wetter Black Sea climate allows summer crops with little irrigation.
Rain-fed sainfoin (korunga) kept three years for hay, then spring wheat uses the nitrogen and the improved soil; common on the eastern plateaus with livestock.
Rye survives the coldest winters and poor soils; an option where winter wheat fails.
A short-season pea replaces fallow on the cold plateaus and adds nitrogen.
Dry pea as a legume break crop between wheat crops.
Winter-sown faba bean, the strongest nitrogen fixer of the pulses, between wheat crops.
Wheat, then second-crop soybean in summer, then maize; the legume second crop replaces second-crop maize.
Livestock farms: silage maize, wheat, then vetch for forage and nitrogen.
Irrigated cold plateaus with livestock: three years of alfalfa for hay, then spring wheat on the improved soil.
